title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
content:
My comment on The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford — Hacker News.

OK, this comment convinced me to give that a shot.

Here's a thing I made in Three.js this morning - a Nudibranch themed Faberge Egg: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (77KB)

I just asked Claude (Opus 5.5 Medium running in regular Claude Chat) to port that to Vanilla JS, in the same thread where it had built it, and got this: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (98KB)

They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414

But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js.

In eyeballing the code I find the Three.js slightly easier to understand myself, but I rarely look at the code for these 3D projects so that isn't a particularly big deal.

title: Jensen Huang Betrayed Nvidia, Not Just His Family
content:
Julian E. Barnes, Tripp Mickle, Paul Mozur, and Maggie Haberman, reporting for The New York Times on Friday:

John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesman, said that the company does not share classified information with its customers, and that customers do not ask Nvidia to press the U.S. government to change its policies on chip sales to China.

He added that the Chinese government had “consistently promoted its own domestic alternatives in China, including Huawei, and strictly limited imports of our data center products.”

Mr. Rizzo has maintained that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were “not unusual” and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.

Turns out this was not true, unless Jensen Huang is consistently banging many of Nvidia’s customers. And it now looks especially bad that an Nvidia spokesman was effectively vouching for the Chinese government’s integrity when it comes to their interest in circumventing the ban against selling them high-end Nvidia hardware.

Liu Chang, a spokesman for the Chinese embassy, said The Times reporting was “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”

Turns out this was completely substantiated and everything it implies about the Chinese government is true.

Ms. Huang has not responded to multiple attempts to reach her for comment in recent days.

The Times has a photo of Ms. Huang with Mr. Huang at a Taipei party in 2024. She’s straight out of Central Casting for a Chinese honeypot.

The New York Times, back on October 29:

Nvidia said the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Jensen Huang’s personal life is his personal life. But he’s made it Nvidia business — an Nvidia spokesman has been repeatedly on the record saying the Huang/Huang relationship was “not unusual”. If you want to cheat on your spouse that’s your business, but it’s irresponsible to allow employees at your company to tell what you know to be lies on your behalf.

Worse would be if it turns out that Megaspeed, the company Alice Huang works (worked?) at, was funneling Nvidia hardware to China in contravention of US national security law. That could make Jensen Huang’s position at Nvidia untenable.

 ★

title: Horible public key tricks:
content:
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"

There is prior art of protest SSL implementations, but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be week, no one would know unless they actually try to break it.

A good protest should be obvious: 

# openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com:443 < /dev/null 2> /dev/null \
    | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color=yes

-----END CERTIFICATE-----

First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent.

The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: 

# Encryption requires knowing e (public)
cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n

The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. 

# Decryption requires knowing d (pivate)
= cyphertext^d mod n

= plaintext^e^d mod n
= plaintext^(e*d) mod n
= plaintext^1 mod n
= plaintext

Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there.

The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus.

My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p.

The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 

58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176
(incrementing until the next prime...)
58174124 * 918491843 = 53432458367670532

As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner.

From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: 

# Single domain
openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request
certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request

# Wildcard
cat > config<<EOF
[ req ]
req_extensions = req_ext

[ req_ext ]
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[ alt_names ]
DNS.1 = *.example.com
DNS.2 = example.com
EOF
openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request
certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request
... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts.

The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated.

Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) avalable charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice.

As for security, this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. I'm not aware of any factoring algorithms that could exploit key selection method, but I can't garantee they don't exist. The method may also produce a p and q that are close together, which makes it possible to easly factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also allow factorisation.

While I wouldn't trust these keys for anything important, they should be perfectly fine for serving a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires man-in-the-middle even if the private key is compromised.

Related:

  • https://tom7.org/httpv/httpv.pdf: [⭐ World's worst TLS server ]
  • /projects/badcert/gen.py: script to generate a vanity key
  • https://rya.nc/cert-tricks.html: More vanity certs
  • https://web.archive.org/web/20230305190629/https://ondergetekende.nl/vanity-rsa-public-key.html: SSH keys.

title: Finite Projective Planes
content:
The idea of finite geometries sounds like an oxymoron the first time you hear of it, something like dry water or cold fire, but the axioms of some kinds of geometry can indeed be satisfied by finite models.

The axioms of projective plane geometry are as follows.

  1. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
  2. Any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.
  3. There exist four points, no three of which are collinear.

The most famous example of a finite projective plane is the Fano plane.

It helps to switch back and forth between thinking of finite geometries geometrically and in terms of set theory. The fact that the Fano plane has an easy-to-understand illustration is fortunate, but not to be taken for granted. Also, it could be misleading to lean to heavily on the fact that the lines and points of finite geometry can, in this case, be represented by points and line segments (and a circle) in the Euclidean plane.

The set-theoretic perspective is that the points are the one-element sets {1}, {2}, …, {7}, and the lines are the sets listed in the legend of the graph: {1, 2, 5}, {1, 3, 7}, …, {5, 6, 7}. It’s simple to confirm that any pair of points lines in exactly one of the three-element sets, that the intersection of any pair of the three-element sets is a one-element set, and that there are three points—1, 2, 3, and 4 will do—such that no three line on the same line, i.e. no three belong to the same three-element set.

The Fano plane is the unique projective plane with 7 points, but there are four non-equivalent projective planes with 10 points.

There are many other examples of non-isomorphic finite projective planes with the same number of points, but there are also many unsettled conjectures, at least as of an hour ago, regarding the existence of finite projective planes of various orders.

Finite geometry might seem like a technicality, spaces that satisfy the axioms but are not what anyone had in mind when the axioms were codified. So why care about finite geometries? For one thing, unexpected examples are quite valuable since they help separate the consequences of a set of axioms from common expectations.

For another, finite geometries come up in applications, such as combinatorics and cryptography. These discrete applications take advantage of intuition from traditional geometry. This intuition is an imperfect guide, so conclusions need to be verified by concrete calculations, but geometric intuition suggests what one ought to verify.

Related posts

  • Misleading plots of elliptic curves
  • Linear systems over finite fields
  • Projective duality

title: Yak-Shaving Overload
content:
Over the years I’ve gotten myself into all varieties of technical rabbit holes and wild goose chases. But I’m feeling weird about my latest trip, involving a forgotten Linux tablet. I blame AI.

Recently, I took on a project that I thought would be a lot of fun … but in the end, I did not like how it made me feel. And I think it reflects the real dangers of leaning too aggressively on AI for stuff you’d like to try out.

A quick explainer: About four years ago, I got a hold of a JingPad, a Linux-based tablet with a massive Achilles’ heel. The problem? It was sold as a Linux-first tablet on ARM, but it was built around an SoC that was not actually particularly open. The Unisoc Tiger T510, as I’ve written, was built for Android, and it has PowerVR graphics that didn’t have an open-source driver. Worse, the company that made it disappeared off the face of the Earth just a handful of months after it first appeared.

The JingPad was a working, fully functional tablet that had been done dirty by its ownership and a bad engineering decision. It was a perfect candidate for the very kind of deconstruction project that has been taking the internet by storm in recent weeks.

So, my goal was this: Let’s see if I can use Claude, Deepseek, Xiaomi MiMo, and other LLMs to get this dang thing working in a modern version of Linux. Certain components, namely the proprietary GPU, might prove difficult, but using Ghidra, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), and a willing-to-go-at-it LLM, it could take things down the road for me.

How hard could it be?

The good, and bad, of an insane yak-shaving project

This is an example of yak-shaving, a concept in which one project gradually evolves into numerous complex branches that never seem to end. For those not familiar, it is based on a Ren & Stimpy skit called “Yak Shaving Day,” which I’ve helpfully embedded above.

Tech projects have a tendency to devolve into wild goose chases like this, as hinted above, this was a whole new beast to me.

Anyway, I want to make clear that this project wasn’t an outright failure. From literally nothing but an empty boot screen, we got the device to load a relatively modern version of Fedora on a “dirty” Linux kernel, based on 6.18. In many ways, it worked, complete with a working touchscreen screen, a charging battery, WiFi access, and an accessible GNOME interface. While not especially fast, I believe it is about as stable as JingOS, the software that came on it in 2022 and itself did not have GPU accelerated graphics.

There were even fun quirks that emerged as I was working on this. I got the flashlight for the camera working on the back, even though there’s literally no use case where it’d actually be useful. And I made significant progress adding FM radio support for the device, despite the fact that, like most mobile devices, FM radio support was never an actual feature of the tool. (In both cases, I thought it would be funny, even though the joke was honestly limited to just me.)

Unfortunately, getting to this point created a project that I would best describe as all-consuming. I had a swarm of different going going at different components, different parts of the device, attempting to scrape details from old firmware versions and related projects in the hope that it’d uncover something missed previously. The result: I had to baby the damn thing all day, managing a bunch of LLMs and rebooting the device as the agents I was using went down one dead-end after another. And shockingly, the thing that kind of made the process less fun and more of a quagmire? It wasn’t the GPU, as I expected; it was the sound.

I got as far as having all the components of the sound card separately working; the DMA chip, the speakers, the codecs, and so on. The GNOME settings app even recognized that the sound card was there. But after receiving something like 50 “this is the last thing before you finally hear sound” messages from DeepSeek, I realized that I had gotten my own brain into a dangerous loop. It was nonstop dopamine hit on top of nonstop dopamine hit—the promise of instant gratification without getting gratified—and after a while, I kind of just felt mentally drained by it all.

This was a “me” project, one that I wanted to see in the world, but in the end it was kind of getting in the way of me thinking about literally anything else.

The way I broke the chain, at least for now, was simple: I put the tablet away for now. I’m going to try my best to get a healthy distance from it. If and when I come back to this project, I want to ensure I’m doing it for reasons that help me learn something rather than stress me out.

In the right context, things like this can be good

This all sounds like a dangerous hobby. But to make the counterargument: For years, we’ve heard stories about smart devices and other objects losing support over time because a company shut down a server somewhere, or chose not to modernize them. With moves like these, we can revive these devices.

For example, the seemingly dead Hackintosh scene has actually seen signs of life, thanks to AI. There’s now a driver for modern-day Nvidia cards on Intel Hackintoshes. It is now possible to boot MacOS on a Snapdragon PC. And Cutefish, a new MacOS-like distro, has promised something previously thought impossible—working graphical MacOS apps in a Linux environment.

A decade ago, when Hackintosh was hitting its peak point in popularity, all this stuff was crazy talk. No way was this going to happen.

And to be clear, there have been other projects I’ve tried that went way better than the one above. As I recently wrote in Boxed News, I was able to turn Dux Shell (formerly Dank Material Shell) into a usable TV computing experience.

Yes, AI is capable of reshaping computing experiences in new ways, in ways that some might find culturally frustrating if the reason you get into tech is because of specific scenes. (I personally don’t, and think the line between cool stuff and gatekeeping is quite small.)

But I’m personally of the view that in cases like the JingPad, where this tablet would be sitting around being useless otherwise, stuff like REA could have genuine value. After all, even if I don’t end up using it to type the next Great American blog post, it can still be useful as a makeshift self-hosting device or even just a lightweight way to surf the web. And I’m hopeful that, eventually, I’ll turn this into a feature-complete device, even with the components that Unisoc and Imagination didn’t bother to make public. However …

Shave yaks? If you value your mental health, pace yourself

If there’s anything I’ve learned about myself over the past decade, I get sucked into different directions way too easily. I can get obsessed with things, and that obsession can sometimes lead to cool places. (See &udm=14.)

But something about the process of attempting to use AI to fix an old tablet felt kind of damaging to a routine in a way that few of my hobbies have over the years. I mentioned Hackintoshing before, and honestly that’s kind of what it reminds me of the most, this attempt to make something do a thing it was never meant to do. But when so much of what you’re doing is working up against something hyping up every action, it’s hard not to feel hollow at the end of it.

As is highlighted by the fact that I publish a little less often these days, I don’t use AI for any of my actual writing. I try taking my time with it. But in a world where it seems like AI is the decorative bird of technology, it can intrude in dangerous ways, with costs that don’t necessarily show themselves right away. And I’m not talking about tokens.

I’m a well-known yak shaver. It’s what I do. This newsletter is a shrine to yak-shaving at the end of the day. But I did not like the way I felt at the end of this week, having hit the reset button on the JingPad for the 250th time. I’m sure I’m not alone here.

My suggestion to anyone else who yak-shaves: Approach agents with caution. After all, an AI agent does not have a limit; you do. Projects like these only take and take your energy, and leave you with a broken-feeling brain.

And unlike a static code window or a page of docs, an agent can make false claims or hype up promises it can’t back up.

Yak-Free Links

Last week was utterly packed with election stuff, which I’ll let you find yourself. But one story you may have missed last week was the death of Salon, one of the digital journalism OGs. Important website that deserved better than an unceremonial shutdown out of nowhere. I’m going to write more about this soon, I think.

I’m sure you haven’t asked yourself what the guy from the “Pretty Fly (for a White Guy)” video has been up to for the past 28 years. But in case you had a poser-shaped hole in your brain, here’s the answer. Fun fact: He still appears on stage at shows for The Offspring sometimes.

As a counterpoint to the above, let me just say that the way that firmware updates have led synth-makers to embrace vibe coding is genuinely interesting to see.

--

Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal! And if you need something weird in your life, I recommend the Tedium Shopping Network.

title: Addition By Subtraction
content:
I still think saying no is important. In that vein, here’s something I shipped by removing functionality (and I think my site is better for it).

For the longest time on my icon gallery sites, you could view a list of icons in four pixel dimensions:

  1. 56×56
  2. 128×128
  3. 256×256
  4. 512×512

Each of these sizes could be accessed via a control on the website. This has been true for years on my site, whether it’s the current site:

Or an older version of the site:

By default, I loaded the 128-pixel version of the icons. But if you wanted to see other sizes, you could.

However, the more I used the site myself the more I thought, “Four options is too many”.

When it comes to choice, what I really wanted was:

  1. Default
  2. Smaller
  3. Bigger

(Plus three is always a good number, unless you have a reason otherwise).

So I removed the big 512 option. If I want to study an icon at that size and detail, I click through to the icon’s detail page.

Now there are three options for list views: 56, 128, and 256. Small (great on mobile), 128 (great by default), and big (let me see more detail).

It’s simple to think about:

  • You get a size by default.
  • Not big enough? Go up a size.
  • Too big? Go down a size.

You don’t need to think about it anymore than that.

I mean you can, but I’ve found I don’t need to. So I’ve taken that off your plate. Less cognitive overhead.

Maybe one day I’ll add a slider and make it all dynamic. But for now, I like this small addition by subtraction.

title: The great software IP writedown
content:
Around a year ago I asked whether the cost of building software had just dropped 90%. A lot has happened since then, and I've become more interested in the knock-on question: if building software is that much cheaper, what is the software itself actually worth?

Was software/SaaS a historic economic anomaly?

One thing that has become obvious to me researching this topic is that software is very much an outlier in terms of ability to extract outsized profit margins, and I think this fact underlines why the industry faces such existential challenges presently.

Typically in history you had three main ways of making "outsized" profits:

Firstly, you had monopolistic behaviour, with Standard Oil being the textbook example. While there are no doubt significant market competition concerns in software and SaaS, I would argue most software businesses, at least by number if not revenue, do not operate in a monopoly.

Secondly, you had network effects, restricting new market entrants. Again, the tech giants clearly do have huge network effect benefits, but many smaller players do not, yet still make very healthy profit margins. Newspapers (used to be) a good example of this, advertisers would want a readership base to advertise to, and if you were starting out from scratch with no readership base, you'd very much struggle to make the commercial model work without willingness to take heavy losses while you built up your readership.

Thirdly you had corruption or using violence to extract high profits out of your customers. Protection money from the mafia is the obvious example historically (though still persists in some geographies). Again, there is an argument that many software companies do achieve their market power via regulatory capture, especially in government contracting. And many would argue regulatory capture is corruption with rounded corners. But again, many software companies don't have a lobbying firm working for them, yet still do very well.

While you can argue that some of these factors are in play for certain tech companies, I struggle to see that the average small or mid-tier SaaS or software company takes advantage of this, yet posts usually extremely high gross (and often net) margins.

So why is this?

Intellectual scarcity

I posit instead that these margins weren't driven by these mechanisms, but instead by simply not enough supply of people able to build software for the demand. And while the number of people able to develop software has exploded over the past 20 or 30 years, the amount of software out there has equally exploded.

So in essence, market actors (whether that would be software engineers or companies) could derive a large amount of value for their work, because there is inherently a (fairly) small pool of people able to build said software.

You can see the issue though now AI agents can do a significant proportion of the engineering. That scarcity is evaporating, which in this model therefore drives the value down sharply. The market always beats margins out of you when there is a shift in supply.

Jevons paradox, though?

Of course, it's not quite as simple as AI agents can do coding, therefore the equilibrium between supply and demand changes. Jevons paradox tells us that when something becomes cheaper and more efficient to use, we often end up using more of it, not less. Jevons' original observation was that more efficient steam engines led to Britain burning more coal, not less. So surely with a huge reduction in cost of bespoke software, we'll see far more demand.

This is true - we're seeing an absolute explosion in the amount of software being created. But I'd argue this software is intrinsically different to what made SaaS (especially) so valuable.

The rough idea with SaaS was that you spent some money on development, and then could sell the same software to thousands or millions of customers. Your marginal cost of a new customer was close to zero, at least in terms of software costs.

But with the Jevons paradox-induced software we have now, it is incredibly bespoke for the most part. Why use a generic CRM when you could build (or purchase) one designed for your exact domain?

I think this dynamic explains the real issue here. Yes, there will be software products in the future. But I suspect these software products will be for the most part far smaller in addressable market size.

Baumol's cost disease

Of course, an argument could be that future software companies operate hundreds or thousands of distinct products, across a whole bunch of markets. There is no doubt with agents this could be from a technology point of view at least more possible than before.

But I think the flaw with this strategy is Baumol's cost disease. When productivity shoots up in one part of the economy, the parts that can't speed up end up getting relatively more expensive. The classic example is a string quartet, which needs the same four musicians and the same amount of time as it did in 1800. Apply that to a software business and the bottleneck moves very quickly from building the product to selling it. Already I'm seeing that while building software has got 10x quicker, sales and marketing is as slow as it always was, at least for most B2B deals.

So I think this explains the flaw with the "software factory" concept that many have been pushing. Yes, you can build hundreds of line-of-business applications in a fraction of the time, if you really want to. But selling these to actual humans is just as hard in my opinion, despite the claims of many that they've managed to automate go to market - any (questionable) efficiencies of these approaches are outweighed by the fact that each buyer has far more marketing directed at them.

I therefore think that there is certainly going to be a market for SaaS in the future - not everyone is going to vibe code their own apps, though some will. But my gut tells me that these are going to be far smaller in scale - and therefore the underlying VC model of throw loads of cash at a SaaS business to scale as fast as possible is even more broken than it was before.

Reproduction

The final thing that is really nagging at me is just how easy it is to copy software now. You can take any agent, give it some screenshots (or if you are even more lazy, a browser tab for it to control) and tell it to clone software you think you like.

We've already seen this on an industrial scale with the ArtCraft suite of clones of everything from Excel to Photoshop.

While I'm sure they are not quite as good or stable as the "genuine" product, this has been the biggest shock to me. Arguably already their Photoshop clone has more features than the unfortunately named GIMP open source clone of Photoshop, which has had 30 years of human effort aimed at it.

So this again makes me wonder where the value in software IP lives. Certainly agents aren't (yet) capable of coming up with good software products to build a business around, so there is definitely value in product taste and choosing the right product to build.

But if you do find a successful niche for your product, it is now trivial for anyone to copy that. So this makes me question exactly where the value is going to lie in future.

One other thing I've noticed is that it's much easier to move between software providers now. Agents can export your data, transform it and import it into a new tool very easily. Even if the provider doesn't offer a nice export, agents are very capable of reverse engineering the web app and doing the export for you anyway. Switching costs have always been one of the quieter moats in SaaS, and that moat is draining too.

The writedown

This is where I think it gets uncomfortable for the finance side.

For the past decade or so, the standard defence of loss-making software companies has been that R&D isn't really an expense. It's an investment. You spend heavily on engineering today, and you get a long-lived asset - the product - that keeps paying out for years.

That logic only holds if the R&D actually builds something durable. If a competitor - or your own customer - can rebuild what you spent five years on in a few weeks with agents, then that spend isn't building an asset at all. It's much closer to a running cost you have to keep paying just to stand still. Which means the underlying economics of a lot of software companies are quite a bit worse than the adjusted numbers suggest.

You can see the same thing from the M&A side. A lot of tech acquisitions were really build-vs-buy decisions. Paying 10x revenue for a startup made sense when building the equivalent in-house would take two years and 30 engineers. But if your own team, with agents, can build it in a matter of weeks, the premium for the technology itself drops to close to zero. You're only paying for the customers and the distribution - and if the product has no real traction, the IP on its own is worth roughly what it would cost to rebuild. Which is not very much anymore.

A year ago I was asking whether the cost of building software had dropped 90%. I think the more uncomfortable question now is whether the value of what's already been built has dropped by a similar amount.
description: Software's outsized margins were built on a scarcity of people who could build it. AI agents are removing that scarcity - so where does the value of software IP go?
